title: The scale
hook: deeds weighed, and good character the heaviest (Tirmidhi)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the book in hand, and your line: the book of deeds. Did your quiet deed go in the book? Today the book's contents are weighed. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-nine.

Some companions of the Prophet, peace be upon him, once laughed at Abdullah ibn Mas'ud. He had climbed a tree, the wind caught his clothes, and his legs showed, thin as sticks. A report in the Musnad of Ahmad says the Prophet asked what they were laughing at, and they said: his thin shins. And he answered that those legs would be heavier on the scale than the mountain of Uhud. Same legs. A different scale. Today, the scale, and what weighs on it.
screen: `THIN LEGS, AND LAUGHTER.` → `HEAVIER THAN A MOUNTAIN.` → `A DIFFERENT SCALE.`

segments.voice: The word is mizan, a balance, a pair of scales. The Qur'an speaks of a just balance set up on the Day of Resurrection, so that no soul is wronged, and says that even the weight of a mustard seed will be brought. Surah al-Qari'ah puts it in two lines: the one whose scales are heavy will have a pleasing life; the one whose scales are light, an abyss. So what is heavy? Here the hadith give an answer. Jami' at-Tirmidhi records the Prophet saying, in paraphrase, that nothing is heavier on the believer's scale on the Day of Resurrection than good character, and that Allah dislikes the one who is foul and coarse in speech. Not the longest night prayer. Not the largest gift. Good character. Another hadith in the same collection says that by good character a person reaches the rank of one who fasts and prays. Arabic has a word for it, husn al-khuluq, beauty of character: patience in traffic, gentleness with a slow parent, honesty when nobody would know. And there's another small, heavy thing. Sahih al-Bukhari closes with a hadith about two phrases, light on the tongue, heavy on the scale, beloved to the Most Merciful: subhan Allah wa bihamdihi, subhan Allah al-'azim. Glory be to Allah and His is the praise; glory be to Allah, the Mighty. Put it together and the scale works the opposite way from the world. The world weighs size, money, looks, the legs in the tree. The mizan, in these texts, weighs a soft answer and a remembered God.
screen: `MIZAN: A JUST BALANCE.` · `HEAVY SCALES, LIGHT SCALES.` · `NOTHING HEAVIER THAN GOOD CHARACTER.` · then, large: `LIGHT ON THE TONGUE, HEAVY ON THE SCALE.`

segments.voice: The practice: be good-natured today, starting with a rehearsal. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone whose good nature you've felt, someone who made a hard moment lighter just by how they were. Stay with them for a few breaths. Then look ahead at today. Where are you most likely to be short with someone? A long line, a meeting, a child at bedtime. See that moment coming. Now see yourself meeting it gently: a slower answer, a smile, one kind sentence. If you pray, you can say the two light phrases, subhan Allah wa bihamdihi, subhan Allah al-'azim. If not, rest on the word gentle. The bell holds the time.
Mizan. The balance on which deeds are weighed on the Day; in a hadith in Tirmidhi, nothing on it is heavier than good character. Today's word.
Your line: character is heavy. Today, when you feel a sharp reply rising, pause one breath and choose the gentler one. Tomorrow, the bridge. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Muslims believe deeds will be weighed on the mizan on the Day of Resurrection, and teachers cite the hadith that nothing is heavier on it than good character; the two phrases 'light on the tongue, heavy on the scale' are part of daily remembrance.

trapdoor: what you thought: the scale weighs good deeds against bad, like a ledger.
what it means: a just balance on the Day where even a mustard seed counts, and the heaviest thing is good character.
what a scholar hears: al-Qari'ah's heavy and light scales, Tirmidhi on husn al-khuluq, and Bukhari's closing hadith of two phrases heavy on the scale.
recall: leaving others unable to match it
